content: Certainly. 1. Su et al. (2018) explored intervention strategies aimed at improving nutrition and health behaviors in women prior to conception, emphasizing the critical role of preconception health in maternal and child outcomes. 2. Lytton and Romney (1991) conducted a meta-analysis on the differential socialization practices of parents towards boys and girls, highlighting the nuanced ways in which gender influences parenting behaviors. 3. Jordans and Tol (2015) advocated for a systems-based approach to providing mental health and psychosocial support for children living in areas affected by armed conflict, emphasizing the need for integrated and sustainable interventions. 4. Sameroff (2010) proposed a unified theory of development that integrates the interplay between genetic predispositions (nature) and environmental influences (nurture), offering a dialectical framework for understanding child development. 5. Murphy et al. (2017) developed an integrative model of parenting in war-affected contexts, focusing on the unique challenges and adaptive strategies employed by caregivers raising children in conflict zones. 6. Murphy, Yoshikawa, and Wuermli (2018) examined the implementation of early childhood development programs in humanitarian settings, emphasizing the importance of evidence-based approaches to improve outcomes for vulnerable populations. 7. Bouchane et al. (2018) reviewed early childhood programs tailored for refugee populations, providing insights into the challenges and opportunities for delivering effective interventions in displacement contexts. 8. Black et al. (2008) analyzed the global and regional prevalence of maternal and child undernutrition, detailing its profound health consequences and the urgent need for targeted interventions. 9. Victora et al. (2008) investigated the long-term effects of maternal and child undernutrition on adult health and human capital, underscoring the intergenerational impact of early nutritional deficits. 10. Rollins et al. (2016) outlined the rationale for investing in breastfeeding promotion and detailed the multifaceted strategies required to improve breastfeeding practices globally. 11. Engle and Pelto (2011) discussed the concept of responsive feeding and its implications for policy and program implementation, emphasizing the importance of caregiver-child interactions during feeding. 12. Tomlinson, Cooper, and Murray (2005) examined the mother-infant relationship and attachment patterns in peri-urban South African settlements, highlighting the influence of socio-environmental factors on early bonding. 13. Lucas, Richter, and Daelmans (2018) described the Care for Child Development intervention, which supports responsive caregiving and promotes early childhood development through structured guidance for caregivers. 14. Shonkoff (2012) emphasized the potential of leveraging biological insights into adversity to address the root causes of health and developmental disparities, advocating for early and targeted interventions. 15. De Walque et al. (2017) explored the role of cash transfers in improving child and adolescent development, presenting evidence from the Disease Control Priorities initiative. 16. Maulik and Darmstadt (2007) provided an overview of childhood disability in lowand middle-income countries, addressing screening, prevention, service delivery, legislation, and epidemiological trends. 17. Green et al. (2005) examined the stigma experienced by individuals with disabilities and their families, detailing the impact of labeling, stereotyping, and discrimination on their lives. 18. The World Health Organization (2001) introduced the International Classification of Functioning, Disability, and Health, providing a standardized framework for understanding and addressing disability. 19. Yousafzai, Lynch, and Gladstone (2014) emphasized the need to move beyond prevalence studies by focusing on screening and interventions for children with disabilities in lowand middle-income countries. 20. Reichow et al. (2013) conducted a systematic review of non-specialist psychosocial interventions for children and adolescents with intellectual disabilities or low-functioning autism spectrum disorders, highlighting their effectiveness and limitations. 21. Hamdani et al. (2017) described the WHO Parent Skills Training program for children with developmental disorders and delays, delivered by family volunteers in rural Pakistan, and outlined the study protocol for its evaluation. 22. The World Health Organization (2017) published the Atlas on Children’s Health and the Environment, emphasizing the critical relationship between environmental factors and child health outcomes. 23. The WHO (2017) reported on global progress in drinking water, sanitation, and hygiene, highlighting the ongoing challenges and disparities in access to these essential services. 24. The WHO (2016) addressed the health, development, and well-being benefits of clean household energy, particularly for women and children, in its report Burning Opportunity. 25. The WHO (2017) published Don’t Pollute My Future. detailing the impact of environmental factors on children’s health and advocating for urgent action to mitigate these risks. 26. The National Department of Health (2017) released the National Antenatal Sentinel HIV and Syphilis Survey Report, providing critical data on maternal health in South Africa. 27. Richter et al. (2009) emphasized the importance of strengthening family systems to support children affected by HIV and AIDS, advocating for holistic and family-centered approaches. 28. Sherr and Cluver (2017) highlighted the comorbidity of HIV and depression, discussing the unique challenges posed by this intersection for affected individuals and healthcare systems. 29. Williams et al. (2010) investigated the neurodevelopmental outcomes of HIV-exposed but uninfected infants, focusing on the effects of in utero antiretroviral exposure. 30. UNAIDS (2017) reported on global progress towards the 90-90-90 targets for ending AIDS, emphasizing the need for sustained efforts to achieve these ambitious goals. 31. Cooper et al. (1999) examined the relationship between postpartum depression and mother-infant interactions in South African peri-urban settlements, highlighting the implications for infant development. 32. Fisher et al. (2012) conducted a systematic review of the prevalence and determinants of common perinatal mental disorders in women from lowand lower-middle-income countries. 33. Ramchandani et al. (2005) explored the impact of paternal depression during the postnatal period on child development, presenting findings from a prospective population study. 34. Howard et al. (2014) reviewed non-psychotic mental disorders in the perinatal period, discussing their prevalence, risk factors, and implications for maternal and child health. 35. Murray (1992) investigated the effects of postnatal depression on infant development, emphasizing the critical need for early identification and intervention. 36. Rahman et al. (2004) examined the impact of maternal depression on infant nutritional status and illness, presenting findings from a cohort study in Pakistan. 37. Rahman et al. (2008) evaluated a community health worker-delivered cognitive behavioral therapy intervention for mothers with depression in rural Pakistan, demonstrating its effectiveness in improving maternal and infant outcomes. 38. Rahman et al. (2013) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of interventions for common perinatal mental disorders in women from lowand middle-income countries. 39. Barlow et al. (2002) performed a meta-analysis of parenting programs, demonstrating their effectiveness in improving maternal psychosocial health. 40. Stoltenborgh et al. (2013) reviewed the prevalence of child neglect, emphasizing the need for greater attention to this critical issue in child welfare. 41. Danese et al. (2009) investigated the long-term health consequences of adverse childhood experiences, including their association with depression, inflammation, and metabolic risk factors. 42. Norman et al. (2012) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the long-term health effects of child abuse and neglect, highlighting the profound and lasting impact on survivors. 43. Burrows et al. (2018) introduced the WHO Violence Prevention Information System, an interactive platform for disseminating scientific findings on violence prevention. 44. Butchart et al. (2014) presented the Global Status Report on Violence Prevention, providing a comprehensive overview of efforts to address violence worldwide. 45. Marmot (2016) emphasized the importance of intersectoral and interagency collaboration for promoting health and well-being, particularly in the WHO European Region. 46. Shekar et al. (2016) outlined an investment framework for achieving global nutrition targets, emphasizing the foundational role of nutrition in development. 47. Gustafsson-Wright et al. (2016) discussed outcome-based financing mechanisms for early childhood development, highlighting their potential to improve program effectiveness. 48. Ertem et al. (2008) provided a guide for monitoring child development in lowand middle-income countries, emphasizing the importance of early detection and intervention. 49. Ertem et al. (2018) compared child development trajectories across four countries, identifying similarities and differences by sex and age in a cross-sectional observational study. 50. Every Woman Every Child (2016) developed an indicator and monitoring framework for the Global Strategy for Women’s, Children’s, and Adolescents’ Health, emphasizing the importance of tracking progress towards 2030 goals.
